Hub C sits among the best-connected nodes and scores 0.55, ahead of D 0.46 and B 0.45, while the tail fades from F 0.15 to G 0.05." width="100%"} Eigenvector centrality measures node importance based on connections to other important nodes. It's the principal eigenvector of the adjacency matrix, computed via power iteration: `x = λ⁻¹ · A · x` A node has high eigenvector centrality if it's connected to other nodes that themselves have high centrality. Unlike degree centrality, it accounts for the quality (not just quantity) of connections. The computation starts with every node at `1`, repeatedly replaces each node's score with the sum of its neighbors' scores plus its own score (that is, it iterates with `A + I`, as NetworkX does), and rescales the vector to unit Euclidean length. Adding the node's own score leaves the eigenvectors unchanged but breaks the tie between the eigenvalues `λ` and `-λ` that every bipartite graph (trees, stars, even cycles) has, so the scores settle instead of oscillating. It stops when the scores change by less than `tol=` between rounds or after `max_iter=` rounds. Typical uses include: - finding influential people in social networks, where knowing well-connected people matters more than knowing many people - ranking proteins, genes, or species by their embedding in densely connected modules - weighting nodes for visualizations that should emphasize the network's core Some caveats: - edge weights are ignored - in a directed graph a node's score is the sum of the scores of the nodes it points *to* (its successors), so nodes that point at important nodes rank highly. On acyclic directed graphs the principal eigenvector is degenerate and the result is not meaningful; consider `katz_centrality()` or `pagerank()` instead - graphs whose two largest eigenvalues are close (large grids, long paths, big random trees) converge slowly. If `max_iter=` runs out before the scores settle, a `RuntimeWarning` is emitted and the last round's scores are returned; raise `max_iter=` to refine them - for a disconnected graph the scores tend to concentrate on the component with the largest eigenvalue ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of power-iteration rounds. Defaults to `100`. If the scores have not converged by then, the values from the last round are returned and a `RuntimeWarning` is emitted. Increase it for large graphs, graphs with a small spectral gap, or when using a very small `tol=`. [tol]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1e-06]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Convergence threshold. Iteration stops once the sum of absolute changes in the (normalized) scores between two consecutive rounds falls below `tol=`. Defaults to `1e-6`. Larger values stop earlier with less precise scores. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name to store eigenvector centrality scores in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), automatically uses `eigen_centrality`. Overwrites column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns the scores as a dictionary without writing anything to the graph. If `False` (default), stores them in the node DataFrame under `attr_name=` and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to centrality scores, normalized so that their squares sum to `1`. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~katz_centrality`) : A version that works on directed acyclic graphs. [](`~pagerank`) : A version with teleportation, for directed graphs. [](`~hub_centrality`) : Hubs and authorities for directed graphs. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A triangle (A, B, C) has a pendant node D attached to C. C scores highest: it has the most neighbors and they are well connected. D has only one neighbor, but because that neighbor is C it still gets a fair score: ::: {#d50a47c7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D")] ) graph.eigen_centrality().get_node_df().select("label", "eigen_centrality") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Well connected to the well connected In *Les Misérables*, two characters are linked when they appear in the same chapter. Gavroche, not Valjean, has the top score here, and most of the others near the top are the students at the barricade, who all appear with one another: ::: {#9e3bcb62 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl lesmis = ec.les_miserables().eigen_centrality().pagerank().cmty_louvain() ( lesmis.get_node_df() .with_columns( pagerank_rank=pl.col("pagerank").rank("min", descending=True) ) .select("label", "degree", "eigen_centrality", "pagerank_rank") .sort("eigen_centrality", descending=True) .head(8) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

PageRank splits a node's rank among its links, so a crowded circle gains less from itself, and it has three of the barricade group in its top ten; eigenvector centrality has eight. Colored by community, the scores pile up in one of them: ::: {#59c2bd25 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} lesmis.plot( color_by="cmty_louvain", size_by="eigen_centrality", label_by="label", seed=3, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### How far the score reaches A node's score is the sum of its neighbors' scores divided by the largest eigenvalue, so it falls off fast away from the densest part of a graph. On a five-node clique with a five-node tail, eigenvector centrality is divided by about four with each step down the tail, while PageRank keeps the tail close to the clique: ::: {#40162be3 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} lollipop = ( ec.Graph().add_lollipop_graph(m=5, n=5).eigen_centrality().pagerank() ) lollipop.get_node_df().select("label", "eigen_centrality", "pagerank") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
